title: The Volume Gap at Five-Valent Vertices
description:
Whether the volume operator of loop quantum gravity has a spectral gap had been addressed at valence four semiclassically, numerically and at leading order in the spins, and at valence five and higher only numerically: Brunnemann and Rideout observed that some embeddings produce eigenvalues accumulating at zero and others do not, and that the decaying ones are exactly those whose reduced sign factors contain ±4. We explain this rule for the Ashtekar–Lewandowski operator and prove most of it in the convention in which spins are assigned to the edges of a fixed embedding. Up to relabelling, every five-valent vertex operator whose edge tangents are in general position (no three coplanar) is zero or −4i[α J1·(J2×J3) + β J1·(J4×J5)] with (α, β) ∈ {(2,0), (2,2), (4,2)}, and “contains ±4” means t = β/α = ½. One direction of the rule is proved in full: for every |t| ∉ {0, 1} the gap closes, through a dimerised chain with two edge modes, exponentially in the spin; at the Ashtekar–Lewandowski value t = ½ the rate is ≍ N3/2 2−N. The other direction is proved for t = 0, where the gap is exactly 2√3, and in part for t = 1: there the gap is proved when the distinguished spin is ½, 1, 3/2 or 2, on every tuple in which three of the other four spins are at most 3 (where it grows linearly in the distinguished spin with the sharp slope 4√(10 − 6√2)), and on several further infinite classes, and it is certified for all spins up to 19. The rest of t = 1 is stated as a conjecture: a uniform gap, growing with that slope in the distinguished spin and like M/ln M in the largest spin, for which we prove the upper bound. In Brunnemann and Rideout's own convention, with the spins sorted, the decay is proved for 6 of the 60 sign vectors (up to sign) that contain ±4.

Along the way we prove the sharp four-valent law λ2 ≥ jmax(jmax+1)/4 for the nonzero eigenvalues λ of J1·(J2×J3), whose constant and minimisers Brunnemann and Thiemann found numerically, through a factorisation into a hydrogen Stark matrix; a factorial gap closing at a six-valent vertex in general position; and a uniform gap for the Rovelli–Smolin operator on every five-valent vertex with an edge of spin ½, which includes the vertices on which we prove that the Ashtekar–Lewandowski gap closes. What is new is the proofs, the mechanisms and the sharp constants. The computer-assisted steps are exact rational, interval, or rigorously bounded floating-point certificates, and all ship with replayable scripts.
